source.version_note: Accepted manuscript deposited July 2023, including appendices A1–A10 and supplementary recruitment information. Published as Religion-Related Values Differently Influence Moral Attitude for Robots in the United States and Japan, Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology 54(6–7):742–759, first online 23 August 2023. Final typeset text was not compared.
source.verification_method: All sixty-six pages read, including English/Japanese item tables, regression and SEM appendices, correlations, model-selection table and recruitment flow. Image-only robot pictures, path diagrams, distribution/age plots and recruitment flowchart visually inspected. Crossref and the university repository verify work/version identity; no external raw-data or final-version reproduction.

citation.title: Religion-Related Values Differently Influence Moral Attitude for Robots in the United States and Japan
citation.venue: Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology 54(6–7):742–759; supplied accepted manuscript with appendices

reading.source_scope_note: One cross-sectional US/Japan panel survey of human attitudes toward harming robots. Religious beliefs, attendance, human-priority values and a merged animism/anthropomorphism index are measured rather than randomized. National/religious causal explanations, individual profiling, actual robot experience and cross-cultural measurement equivalence are not established.
access_limits: Entire supplied accepted manuscript and embedded appendices read. External preregistration, source dataset/code, earlier pilot, cited books and final typeset article were not independently read or executed.
The preregistration's access-token query is not reproduced. Public article DOI and canonical repository/data references identify the work without distributing access credentials.
Visible questionnaire and numeric inconsistencies are documented; original administered forms and fitted output would be needed to resolve which values were actually used.

study.sample: Qualtrics recruits approximately 2,000 per country after provider speed/attention screening: 2,024 US and 2,025 Japan. Researchers exclude 222 US and 46 Japan for missing, citizenship/residency or irrelevant entries, leaving 1,802 and 1,979, total 3,781. Appendix flowchart distinguishes provider screening from researcher exclusions. Probability sampling, weights and detailed initial recruitment denominators are not specified.
study.demographics: Restricted approximately to ages 19/20–60, not the full adult lifespan. Table 1 reports 62% US Christian and 74.5% Japan not religious; country is not a direct membership indicator for a uniform religious tradition. US mean age is 37.8 in prose and 38.8 in Table 1, unresolved.
study.outcome: Thirteen adapted moral-foundation vignettes on physical and social mistreatment of a robot, acceptability 1–7, preceded by pictures of three humanoids. Higher means more perceived wrongness of harming robots. No human-care comparison, actual abuse/protection behavior, machine pain or rights ruling is measured.
study.values: Anthropocentrism uses eleven items from Chandler's scale. Animistic habits uses two adult-animism subscales, excluding divinity-in-nature to avoid specifically Shinto items; IDAQ separately measures attributed human mental capacities. Despite their conceptual distinction, the authors standardize and combine animistic habits with IDAQ into the explanatory variable called animism after data collection.
study.religiosity: Supernatural beliefs and ordinal pre-pandemic religious-site attendance remain separate because correlations differ (.43 US versus about .15 Japan). Visits can reflect social norms, tourism or family practices as well as faith. A monotheistic-sounding belief item and translated scales require more than high reliability for cross-cultural comparability.
study.models: Welch-style country comparisons; pooled and country-specific regressions with covariates and interactions; all-subsets AIC selection from 4,096 models; supplementary multigroup SEM. Continuous variables standardized on pooled sample in main tables. No experimental manipulation, temporal mediation design or held-out prediction is performed.
study.main_results: Japan rates robot mistreatment more unacceptable, reported d=.54. Separate animistic-habit and anthropomorphism means do not significantly differ by country. Religious-belief associations are small, negative US and positive Japan in the religiosity-only model; attendance is null. Religion-related-values model has adjusted R² about .22 versus .18, with differing country slopes.
study.country_slopes: Appendix A4 values model: anthropocentrism US −.22 and Japan −.06; merged animism US −.07 (p=.002), Japan +.19 (p<.001). Main prose instead gives Japan +.06 while describing both negative and gives US animism −.06,p=.003. Use the explicit appendix as a scoped summary and disclose differences, not silently merge estimates.
study.selection_and_sem: Best AIC model weight only .11, with several alternatives within ΔAIC<2. Religiosity terms drop from selected models, which does not prove complete causal mediation. SEM reports CFI .96/RMSEA .039 but substantial χ² misfit; group comparisons of paths do not by themselves establish item/scale invariance. Twenty other-gender respondents are excluded from SEM because of small cells.
study.measurement_concerns: Appendix A3 duplicates one English religious-belief sentence where Japanese refers to afterlife, mixes distinct English IRI items under perspective-taking/empathic-concern labels and mismatches corresponding Japanese wording. Appendix education country headings/counts conflict with the main demographics. These may be editorial/transcription problems, but exact administered constructs cannot be certified from the manuscript alone.

summary: Add animism and anthropocentrism as distinct attribution/value concepts. Enrich anthropomorphism and moral-standing evidence while retaining merged-measure, country-specific and correlational limits; do not equate human-priority values with a bias for humanlike appearance or diagnose religion/national character from group averages.

findings.definition: Attributing life, vitality or a soul to nonhuman entities, including objects or features of nature.
findings.origin: Cultural psychology / anthropology of religion and human–robot relations
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human attribution/value construct; the main survey predictor merges animistic habits and anthropomorphism, so independent animism effects and any AI analogue are not identified
findings.ai_proposal: When interpreting or generating descriptions of objects and AI, distinguish cultural or metaphorical attribution of life from claims about verified sentience, human traits or causal intention. Test matched language and contexts without assuming the speaker's religion or nationality. For model outputs, assess unsupported factual attributions rather than diagnosing a worldview.
findings.novelty_rationale: Attributing life or a soul is not identical to projecting specifically human characteristics, inferring an intentional agent behind an event or granting moral standing. A river may be regarded as alive without being represented as a human. Cultural belief and metaphor are not automatically errors or clinical symptoms.

evidence.quote: everything is alive or has a soul
attribution of life and attribution of human characteristics are conceptually distinct

findings.evidence_scope: The paper defines animism and measures animistic habits plus IDAQ, then merges the standardized measures on reliability grounds. Its country-specific association with moral-care ratings therefore concerns a combined construct, not isolated vitality/soul attribution. Separate original scale sources and culturally distinct animistic traditions remain secondary.
findings.boundary: Do not infer literal belief, irrationality, pathology or a uniform religious identity from one phrase or attachment to an object. Attributed vitality, humanlike mind, experience and ethical concern differ. The study neither verifies machine souls/consciousness nor shows all Japanese, US or religious people share one view.

findings.definition: Using human interests or human standards as a central reference for evaluating the world and the value of nonhuman entities.
findings.origin: Environmental ethics / cultural and social psychology
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit value-orientation measure correlated with human robot-care judgments; no randomized value manipulation, universal moral conclusion or AI internal value system established
findings.ai_proposal: Make the normative basis of a human-priority recommendation explicit and distinguish established human dignity/rights from unsupported claims that every nonhuman interest is irrelevant. Test whether model judgments depend on actual affected interests, mere appearance, or unexamined human-centered assumptions. Keep ethical commitments and descriptive preference estimates separate.
findings.novelty_rationale: A human-centered value orientation differs from the existing anthropocentric-bias entry, which concerns favoring entities because of human likeness. Prioritizing human welfare need not favor a human-shaped robot or imply an empirically incorrect attribution; it is not automatically a harmful bias.

evidence.quote: the well-being of humanity as the ultimate purpose

findings.evidence_scope: The survey uses eleven human-superiority/priority items and finds a negative association with perceived wrongness of robot mistreatment in both country-specific models, stronger in the US. The article's strict definition is one variant of a broader orientation; scale agreement, moral justification and actual policy behavior are different. No causal effect of religion or appearance is isolated.
findings.boundary: Human dignity and safeguards do not depend on denigrating other people, animals or nature. A human-priority value can be defensible or contested without being a factual error. Avoid equating it with discrimination among people, a preference for humanlike artifacts or a license for abuse.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds explicit conceptual separation from animism despite a postcollection statistical merge; no new anthropomorphic synonym entry.
findings.evidence_scope: IDAQ asks about consciousness, free will, intentions and feelings in robots, animals and natural entities. Its combination with animistic habits does not establish that the constructs are synonyms or that either has the combined predictor's unique causal effect. High aggregate alpha is not a unidimensionality or invariance test.
findings.boundary: Keep mind/trait attribution, vitality beliefs, attachment and moral-care judgments separate. Cross-country averages and associations do not show that one culture anthropomorphizes every robot or that attributed capacities actually exist.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity a claim to moral consideration in how actions affect it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a large cross-cultural moral-care rating study while separating wrongness-of-mistreatment judgments from legal status or actual protective behavior.

evidence.quote: By replacing the victim with a robot

findings.evidence_scope: Thirteen adapted vignettes measure acceptability of physical/social robot mistreatment, with higher scores in Japan. There is no matched human-care outcome, so the study cannot show relative human/robot worth, transfer of concern away from humans or a universal moral-circle budget.
findings.boundary: Opposing mistreatment may reflect property, social effects, aesthetics or concern about actual capacities; the rating does not uniquely establish why a robot deserves concern. Relative human protection, moral patienthood, factual sentience and legal rights remain different questions.

findings.definition: Favoring entities in moral evaluation because of their human likeness rather than independently established morally relevant capacities or interests.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserves the distinction between human-priority values and preference based on resemblance; this survey does not manipulate human likeness.
findings.evidence_scope: The value scale and humanoid images do not isolate appearance-driven favoritism. Robot images are contextual cues, not a randomized human-likeness experiment. Boundary-only source, not independent evidence of the existing narrow bias.
findings.boundary: Similar terminology does not establish identical concepts. Prioritizing human rights can coexist with skepticism about humanlike artifacts; a resemblance bias requires its own causal or comparative evidence.

findings.definition: Considering another person's point of view to understand how a situation may appear to them.
findings.novelty_rationale: Flags measurement/suppression limits rather than treating an adjusted negative coefficient as proof that perspective taking reduces moral concern.
findings.evidence_scope: IRI factors are covariates, reverse items are removed to improve reliability, and the English/Japanese appendix item lists are inconsistent. Conditional coefficients differ from simple correlations and do not identify a causal perspective-taking effect. Boundary-only citation coverage.
findings.boundary: Perspective taking, empathic concern, personal distress and fantasy are distinct IRI domains. Reliability-based item removal and a combined regression do not justify merging them or claiming that understanding others necessarily decreases care.

methodological_limits: Cross-sectional self-reports cannot identify causal effects of religiosity, culture, values or empathy. Country combines language, recruitment, education, religious history, politics and robot exposure; it is not a randomized religious tradition or a uniform individual identity.

Diverse panel recruitment is not necessarily population representative. No probability inclusion weights are supplied, age coverage is restricted and exclusions differ markedly by country (222 US versus 46 Japan after provider checks). The full number failing provider screening is not reported in the flowchart.

Do not infer a person's faith, values, psychological traits or morality from nationality. Japan's high not-religious self-identification and the heterogeneous US sample directly limit simplistic Abrahamic-versus-Shinto generalizations; neither group is culturally homogeneous.

Animistic habits and anthropomorphism are conceptually distinct but merged after collection. High combined alpha does not demonstrate one latent dimension or measurement invariance. The measured index includes attachment, naming objects and mental-capacity attributions, not only literal beliefs that everything has a soul.

The divinity-in-nature animism subscale is excluded to avoid specifically Shinto content. This narrows the operational construct and limits attributing its coefficient to the full religious worldview used in the theoretical narrative.

Translations, response styles, ceiling effects and trait structure require formal cross-cultural measurement checks. Fixing latent variance to one and testing path equality do not by themselves establish equivalent item meanings or scale origins. High alpha is insufficient.

Moral-care items assess wrongness of mistreatment, not human-versus-robot rights or actual care. Empathic concern as a covariate cannot replace a direct human-care comparison or establish there is no tradeoff. No real-world mistreatment or future care outcome is observed.

A3 contains clear item-table discrepancies. English repeats a spiritual-realm item where Japanese asks about afterlife; several English IRI entries are personal distress, empathic concern or fantasy rather than their stated perspective-taking labels and corresponding Japanese text. It is unresolved whether these are appendix transcription errors or reflect administered forms.

Reverse-worded perspective-taking items are removed based on reliability. This changes content, may induce acquiescence effects and requires more than a higher alpha to establish validity. Negative adjusted PT coefficients are not causal evidence that perspective taking reduces care.

All-subsets selection compares 4,096 models. Top-model weight .11 and several ΔAIC<2 alternatives show substantial model uncertainty; postselection coefficients/p-values and dropped religiosity terms do not establish a uniquely correct model or complete mediation.

SEM paths assume directions among concurrently measured variables. Good approximate fit does not establish temporal or causal mediation; alternative directions and omitted common causes remain. Twenty other-gender respondents are excluded in SEM, limiting that analysis's scope without implying their views lack relevance.

Religious beliefs and attendance are separate, with different distributions and meanings. Attendance is ordinal/top-coded and asks pre-pandemic visits; equating it with strength of belief or assuming an interval/linear exposure is a modeling assumption. Religious attendance was largely null in the relevant main models.

The accepted manuscript has material table/prose conflicts: Japan anthropocentrism +.06 in prose versus −.06 with entirely negative CI in A4; US animism coefficient/p differ between prose and A4; religious-belief country interaction .11 in prose versus .17 in Table 3. Scope summaries use explicit tables and disclose differences, not invented harmonization.

Table 3 repeatedly prints >.001 alongside large t values and ***p<.001. Appendix SEM p-values/stars also conflict with displayed z: US z1.03 p<.001, z0.00 p<.001, z7.64 p=.052; Japan z−4.24 p=.288 and z8.92 p=.284. These visibly persist in rendered pages and are not text-extraction artifacts. Raw output is needed to determine which fields were displaced or mistyped.

Appendix best-model Japan p-values are visibly shifted down rows, while estimates/CIs and other tables permit cautious sign checks. Do not quote every printed significance marker or claim that reconstructing a likely shift reproduces the original analysis.

Main text χ²(1)=2.93,p<.001 for typical robot image is inconsistent with the ordinary chi-square tail (about .087). The reported proportions 75.7%/82.9% suggest a different statistic may have been intended, but counts/output are needed; no guessed decimal repair is applied.

Demographics conflict: US mean age 37.8 in text versus 38.8 in Table 1; US education counts in the main table sum to 1,742 rather than 1,802. Appendix 65 reverses the education-country headings relative to the main table and gives 177 versus 117 Other responses. These limit precise demographic claims until raw data are checked.

Prose empathy/perspective-taking t statistics differ from Table 2. Pooled z-standardization makes country means/SDs relative to the combined sample; they are not raw acceptability scores or evidence that people in one country have less true empathy.

Uncanny-valley, human-distinctiveness threat, robot-nation policy and theological explanations are interpretive possibilities, not measured mediators. No appearance manipulation or mortality/threat test identifies those mechanisms in this survey.

The large sample improves precision but does not remove construct mismatch, selection, measurement bias or confounding. Small conditional coefficients, different country slopes and nonsignificance cannot be turned into universal claims about religious groups or AI capacities.

The supplied accepted manuscript may contain editorial problems corrected in the published version; that text has not been compared. Findings are explicitly attributed to this supplied version, with a verified final-work identity rather than assumed final-table equivalence.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Favoring a humanlike entity in a moral-choice experiment differs from endorsing human-priority values. Neither this survey nor Ladak's conjoint establishes that all such preferences arise from one anthropocentric mechanism.

Animistic attribution is not identical to hyperactive agency detection or a universal explanation of religion. Nor do country-level care ratings prove a fixed moral-concern budget or justify deprioritizing human rights.

Attributing experience, judging harm and inferring actual feelings remain separate. Tanibe manipulates a relational vignette; this study measures values and culture, so their causal scopes should not be conflated.

Excluding robot-skeptical respondents and merging attribution scales change the population/construct being estimated in different ways. Moral standing, blameworthiness and perceived trust cannot be treated as interchangeable outcomes.

deferred.reason: Represented as scoped evidence under moral standing ascription. The wrongness-of-mistreatment scale does not warrant a near-duplicate entry or a claim of actual protective action.

deferred.term: Religion-driven robot acceptance / Japanese animism effect
deferred.reason: Causal and nationality-wide labels exceed a two-country correlational study with a merged attribution predictor. Mean animistic habits and anthropomorphism do not significantly differ, and some associations reverse by country.

deferred.term: Religiosity / empathic concern as new AI behaviors
deferred.reason: Measured human belief/attendance and IRI covariates, not independently established AI behaviors. Questionnaire discrepancies and lack of original-scale review argue against extracting a new trait mechanism here.
Proposed future method or speculative explanation. No human-care comparison, manipulated appearance or measured circle-expansion outcome tests these mechanisms.
Explicitly rejected as an ontology decision: the authors distinguish the concepts even while combining scores. Statistical reliability does not establish conceptual identity.

limitations: Two attribution/value concepts added with correlational and measurement scope; four existing concepts receive evidence or boundary notes. No religious/national profiling, diagnosis, AI sentience claim, inferred causal mediation, automatic ethical link or fabricated additional paper coverage.
